title: Five causes of every act
hookLine: Krishna counts five causes behind every act, and the doer is only one
carry: the doer is one cause of five
tomorrow: Three kinds of seeing and doing
last: TYAGA — LET GO OF THE FRUIT.

cards: Back in chapter eleven, Krishna showed Arjuna his cosmic form. Inside it, Arjuna saw the great warriors of both armies rushing in, like rivers rushing to the sea. Then Krishna told him: they are already slain by me.
Be only the instrument, Arjuna. Until then, Arjuna had talked as if the whole war hung on him alone: my bow, my sin, my choice.
Now, in the last chapter, Krishna takes any action at all, good or bad, and counts its causes. He finds five. And the doer is only one.

teach.b: Verse thirteen: learn from me the five causes for the completion of every action, as taught in the Samkhya teaching. Verse fourteen lists them.
First, adhishthana, the seat: the body, the base where the action happens. Second, karta, the doer: the one who says I'm doing this. Third, the various instruments: the senses and the mind.
Fourth, the many different efforts: the movements, the breaths, the energies that carry the action out.
And fifth, daiva. Daiva is hard to translate. It can mean the divine, providence, or what some call fate or luck: the part beyond your control.

Different teachers read it differently, some as God's hand, some as the weight of past karma. Verse fifteen: whatever action a person begins with body, speech or mind, right or wrong, these five are its causes.
The one who sees themselves as the only doer, because their understanding is untrained, doesn't see.

teach.h: THE DOER IS ONE OF FIVE.
teach.b: The doer is one cause among five. Some teachers say this cuts two ways. When things go well, it takes the air out of pride: you had help, from your body, your senses, your effort, and something beyond all of them.
When things go badly, it takes some weight off guilt: not everything was yours to control. This is the root of a very Hindu habit: offering the results of what you do to God.
Some devotees say sarvam Krishnarpanam, all of it offered to Krishna, when a task is done.

how: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 18.13–18.16 to loosen the sense of being the sole doer, so that success doesn't feed pride and failure doesn't crush; some devotees offer the results of their actions to God for the same reason.

o: the unseen fifth cause, beyond your control
a lesser god who guards a single village
the doer's own effort and strong willpower

games.q: the five causes — tap the pairs.
p: the fifth: the divine, the unseen

s: the Gita says the doer is the only real cause of an action
the doer is one of five; verse 16 says seeing only yourself is not seeing.
daiva can be read as the divine, providence, or fate
teachers read it differently, some as God's hand, some as past karma.
the five causes apply to actions of body, speech and mind
verse 15: right or wrong, these five are its causes.

games.q: you've just done something brilliant, and everyone's congratulating you. what would Gita 18.16 say?
o: take all the credit: you did it.
you're one cause among five; the one who sees only 'I' doesn't see.
it was only luck, so you did nothing.
games.why: one cause among five. the Gita doesn't erase the doer; it just refuses to make the doer the whole story.

practice: Take one breath as an action and notice the five: the seat, your body sitting; the doer, the sense that I am breathing; the instruments, nose, lungs, attention; the effort, muscles moving, air flowing.
And the fifth, the part you didn't make and can't explain: that there is air, and that you're alive to breathe it. Let the breath keep going on its own.

wordCard.voice: Daiva, the divine, providence or fate. Gita eighteen, fourteen: the fifth of five causes of action, the seat, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and daiva, the unseen fifth. The doer is only one of five.

orig.note: Sanskrit: daiva, of the gods, the divine, providence or fate; the fifth cause of action in Gita 18.14.

carryVoice: Your line: the doer is one cause of five. Not I alone, so the result can be offered. That's two hundred twenty.
